# 🤔 Why Regularize?

## A quick warmup 🎮

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Before we dive in — a fast review of yesterday's ideas.

[👉 I click here… you wait…](https://play.kahoot.it/v2/?quizId=090bbc1e-c963-4f36-9cfb-45f81949c1f3)

> Class imbalance, train/test split, recipes, workflows…
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](https://media.giphy.com/media/kDCargqZQ88Jq/giphy.gif?cid=ecf05e47cql4isfzdq2udvl3cqfh225u0ab93sm4u87alq33&ep=v1_gifs_search&rid=giphy.gif&ct=g){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

---

## The problem with "throw everything at the model" 😬

::: {.incremental}
- YRBS has **40+ predictors** of risky behavior. Many are correlated. Some are noise.
- A plain logistic regression will happily fit a coefficient for *every* one.
- Result → **overfitting**: train metrics look amazing, test metrics flop. 📉
- We need a way to say: *"only keep the predictors that actually matter."*
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## The big idea
**Shrinkage** = pull coefficients toward zero. Some land *exactly* at zero — that's automatic feature selection. 💡
:::
:::

---

## What is "shrinkage"?

::: {.incremental}
- Shrinkage **shrinks** (or zeroes out) the coefficients of predictors.
- It strikes a balance between **fitting the data** and **avoiding overfitting**.
- Smaller coefficients → **less variance** → better generalization to new data.
- The two famous shrinkage methods: **Ridge** and **Lasso**. (Elastic Net = both.)
:::

::: {.footer}
[ISLRv2](https://hastie.su.domains/ISLR2/ISLRv2_website.pdf)
:::

# 📐 The Math (just enough)

## Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Every regression starts here:

$$
\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n\bigg( y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j x_{ij}\bigg)^2
$$

::: {.incremental}
- The **error** between model prediction and actual data.
- Smaller RSS → better fit on the **training** data.
- ⚠️ Minimizing RSS alone is exactly how we overfit.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](img/rss.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

::: {.footer}
[ISLRv2](https://hastie.su.domains/ISLR2/ISLRv2_website.pdf)
:::

# 🔵 Ridge Regression (L2)

## What Ridge does

::: {.incremental}
- Adds a **penalty term** to the RSS: a multiple of the **squared** coefficients.
- The penalty parameter $\lambda$ controls how aggressive the shrinkage is.
- All predictors **stay in the model** — but their coefficients get smaller.
- Also called **L2 regularization**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n\bigg( y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j x_{ij}\bigg)^2}_{\text{RSS (fit)}} + \underbrace{\lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2}_{\text{shrinkage penalty}}
$$
:::

::: {.footer}
[ISLRv2](https://hastie.su.domains/ISLR2/ISLRv2_website.pdf)
:::

---

## Ridge — visually

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](img/ridge_graph.png)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
- $\lambda = 0$ → ordinary least squares.
- $\lambda \to \infty$ → all coefficients squeezed toward (but never *exactly*) zero.
- Ridge **never drops** a predictor.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🎯 Ridge is great when you believe **most predictors contribute a little**.
:::

::: {.footer}
[ISLRv2](https://hastie.su.domains/ISLR2/ISLRv2_website.pdf)
:::

# 🟠 Lasso (L1)

## What Lasso does

::: {.incremental}
- Same idea as Ridge — but the penalty uses the **absolute value** of the coefficients.
- The geometry of the L1 penalty lets coefficients hit **exactly zero**.
- That means **automatic feature selection** built into the model. ✨
- Also called **L1 regularization**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n\bigg( y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j x_{ij}\bigg)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p | \beta_j|
$$
:::

::: {.footer}
[ISLRv2](https://hastie.su.domains/ISLR2/ISLRv2_website.pdf)
:::

---

## Lasso — visually

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](img/lasso_graph.png)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
- $\lambda = 0$ → least-squares fit (everything stays).
- As $\lambda$ grows, predictors are **dropped one by one** (their lines hit 0).
- $\lambda$ *very large* → null model (no predictors at all).
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🎯 Lasso is great when you suspect **only a few predictors really matter**.
:::

::: {.footer}
[ISLRv2](https://hastie.su.domains/ISLR2/ISLRv2_website.pdf)
:::

---

## Ridge vs Lasso — side by side

::: {.panel-tabset}

### 👀 Visual
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Lasso (L1)**
![](img/lasso_graph.png){width="90%"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Ridge (L2)**
![](img/ridge_graph.png){width="90%"}
:::
:::

### 📊 Behavior
| | **Ridge** | **Lasso** |
|---|---|---|
| Penalty | $\sum \beta_j^2$ | $\sum \|\beta_j\|$ |
| Drops predictors? | ❌ never | ✅ yes (some hit 0) |
| Best when | many small effects | few strong effects |
| Bias / variance | small bias, low variance | larger bias, sparser model |
| Interpretability | medium | high (only kept predictors) |

### 🎯 The geometry

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](img/Contours .png){fig-align="center"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.incremental}
- The **ellipses** are RSS contours (small RSS in the middle).
- The **gray region** is where the penalty allows coefficients to live.
- **Ridge = circle** → tangency rarely lands on an axis → no zeros.
- **Lasso = diamond** → tangency *often* lands on a corner → exact zeros. ✨
:::
:::
:::

:::

::: {.footer}
[ISLRv2](https://hastie.su.domains/ISLR2/ISLRv2_website.pdf)
:::

# 🟣 Elastic Net

## Best of both worlds

::: {.incremental}
- Combines **Ridge + Lasso** in one penalty.
- Keeps Lasso's **feature selection** *and* Ridge's **handling of correlated predictors**.
- Controlled by two knobs: `penalty` ($\lambda$) and `mixture` (how much L1 vs L2).
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n\bigg( y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j x_{ij}\bigg)^2 + \lambda_1 \sum_{j=1}^p | \beta_j| + \lambda_2 \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## In `tidymodels`
- `mixture = 1` → pure **Lasso**
- `mixture = 0` → pure **Ridge**
- `0 < mixture < 1` → **Elastic Net**
:::
:::

::: {.footer}
[Practitioner's Guide to Data Science](https://scientistcafe.com/ids/elastic-net.html)
:::

# 🎛️ Picking the Best $\lambda$

## How do we choose $\lambda$?

::: {.incremental}
- $\lambda$ is a **hyperparameter** — you set it *before* training.
- Try a **grid** of candidate values, evaluate each with **cross-validation**.
- Pick the $\lambda$ that maximizes your metric (e.g., **ROC AUC**).
- This is exactly what `tune_grid()` automates for us. 🤖
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 The same `tune()` placeholder + grid pattern works for *every* tunable model in `tidymodels`. Learn it once, reuse forever.
:::

---

# 💻 Lasso with `tidymodels`

## Today's task 🎯

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
> **From 40+ youth-risk-behavior items, which ones best predict whether a teen will text-and-drive?** 📱🚗

::: {.incremental}
- **Outcome**: `TextingDriving` (binary: Yes / No)
- **Predictors**: every other risky-behavior item in YRBS
- **Model**: Lasso logistic regression
- **Why Lasso?** It will *automatically* drop irrelevant predictors and hand us a short list of the strongest signals.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](https://media.giphy.com/media/eGyJz0UnrEy3K/giphy.gif?cid=ecf05e470l48hi14w34gpqwhaddfljk9xuwn2xir0rn52323&ep=v1_gifs_search&rid=giphy.gif&ct=g){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

---

## Setup — load packages 📦

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(MLearnYRBSS)
library(janitor)
library(skimr)
library(vip)

data("riskyBehaviors")
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
## Want help writing the spec?
`usemodels::use_glmnet(TextingDriving ~ ., data = train)` will scaffold the recipe + spec + workflow + grid for you. Copy, paste, adjust. 🤖
:::
:::

---

## 1️⃣ Recode the outcome to binary

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1-3|4-9|10|11-17"
#| output-location: fragment
riskyBehaviors_analysis <-
    riskyBehaviors |>
    mutate(
        TextingDriving = case_when(
            TextingDriving == 1 ~ 0,
            TextingDriving %in% c(2, 3, 4, 5) ~ 1,
            .default = NA
        ),
        TextingDriving = factor(TextingDriving)
    ) |>
    drop_na(TextingDriving) |>
    select(-SourceVaping, -SourceAlcohol, -SexOrientation,
           -DrivingDrinking, -SexualAbuse, -SexualAbuseByPartner,
           -Grade, -Age)
```

---

## What did we just do? 🤔

::: {.incremental}
- 🎯 **Outcome encoding:** `0` = never texted-and-drove · `1` = at least once.
- 🚨 We'll target the **second level** (`1`) when computing ROC.
- 🧹 We **dropped** redundant or post-event columns (e.g. `DrivingDrinking`) to avoid leakage.
:::

# 2️⃣ Split + Resample

## Train / test split — stratified

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|3-4|6-7|9"
#| output-location: fragment
set.seed(1990)

analysis_split <- initial_split(
    riskyBehaviors_analysis,
    strata = TextingDriving
)

analysis_train <- training(analysis_split)
analysis_test <- testing(analysis_split)

analysis_split
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Always `strata =` the outcome
Keeps the class balance roughly equal in train and test. **Critical** when the outcome is imbalanced.
:::
:::

---

## Sanity check — class balance

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Training**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
analysis_train |>
    tabyl(TextingDriving) |>
    adorn_pct_formatting(0) |>
    adorn_totals()
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Testing**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
analysis_test |>
    tabyl(TextingDriving) |>
    adorn_pct_formatting(0) |>
    adorn_totals()
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
> Both sets show the same proportions — `strata =` did its job. ✅
:::

---

## Cross-validation folds

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|3"
#| output-location: fragment
set.seed(1990)

analysis_folds <- vfold_cv(analysis_train, v = 5, strata = TextingDriving)
analysis_folds
```

::: {.fragment}
> **5 folds** of the *training* set. Each candidate $\lambda$ will be evaluated on all 5 — the test set stays sacred.
:::

# 3️⃣ Recipe + Spec + Workflow

## Recipe (preprocessing)

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1-2|3|4|5|6|7"
#| output-location: fragment
texting_rec <-
    recipe(TextingDriving ~ ., data = analysis_train) |>
    step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
    step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    step_impute_mean(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

texting_rec
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## `step_normalize()` is **mandatory** for Lasso 🚨
Lasso penalizes coefficients on the same scale. Without normalization, predictors measured in larger units get unfairly shrunk. Don't skip it.
:::
:::

---

## Model spec — `glmnet` 🌱

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1-3|4|6"
#| output-location: fragment
texting_spec <-
    logistic_reg(
        penalty = tune(), # ⬅️ we'll tune this
        mixture = 1 # ⬅️ pure Lasso
    ) |>
    set_engine("glmnet")

texting_spec
```

---

## The `mixture` knob 🎛️

::: {.callout-tip}
## One spec, three models
- `mixture = 1` → **Lasso** 🟠
- `mixture = 0` → **Ridge** 🔵
- `0 < mixture < 1` → **Elastic Net** 🟣
:::

::: {.fragment}
> Want Elastic Net? `mixture = tune()` and let CV pick the best blend.
> [📖 Read the docs](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/reference/glmnet-details.html)
:::

---

## Workflow — bundle them 🔗

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|3|4"
#| output-location: fragment
texting_wf <-
    workflow() |>
    add_recipe(texting_rec) |>
    add_model(texting_spec)

texting_wf
```

::: {.fragment}
> Same shape as yesterday's logistic regression. **Only the spec changed.** ✨
:::

# 4️⃣ Tune the Penalty

## What's a tuning grid?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- A **list of candidate** $\lambda$ values to try.
- For each value, `tidymodels` fits the model on every CV fold.
- The grid lives on the **log scale** because $\lambda$ ranges over many orders of magnitude.
- Then we pick the $\lambda$ with the best metric.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](img/grid.gif){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

---

## Three flavors of grid

![](https://dials.tidymodels.org/logo.png){.absolute top=0 right=0 width=80 height=90}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Manual
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
glmnet_grid <- data.frame(penalty = 10^seq(-6, -1, length.out = 20))
glmnet_grid
```
A simple log-spaced sequence — quick and dirty.

### Wide range
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
penalty_grid <- grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-4, 4)), levels = 50)
penalty_grid
```
A custom range you supply — useful when you've explored before.

### Recommended
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
lambda_grid <- grid_regular(penalty(), levels = 50)
lambda_grid
```
The default `penalty()` range from `dials` — sensible defaults, no thinking needed. ⭐

:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 Start with the **recommended** version. Only get fancy if your tuning curve looks weird.
:::

---

## How do you "see" the grid?

![](img/grid_search_2.png){fig-align="center" width="65%"}

::: {.footer}
[ISLR tidymodels labs](https://emilhvitfeldt.github.io/ISLR-tidymodels-labs/06-regularization.html)
:::

---

## Run the tuning ⚙️

![](https://tune.tidymodels.org/logo.png){.absolute top=0 right=0 width=80 height=90}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|3|5-10"
#| output-location: fragment
doParallel::registerDoParallel()

set.seed(2023)

lasso_tune <-
    tune_grid(
        object = texting_wf,
        resamples = analysis_folds,
        grid = lambda_grid,
        control = control_resamples(event_level = "second")
    )

doParallel::stopImplicitCluster()
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Behind the scenes
Each row of the grid → fit on every CV fold → average performance. With `levels = 50` and `v = 5` that's **250 model fits** — `doParallel` keeps it snappy. 🚀
:::
:::

---

## Collect the metrics

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
lasso_tune |>
    collect_metrics()
```

---

## Visualize the metrics

::: {.panel-tabset}

### autoplot
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
autoplot(lasso_tune)
```

### Custom ggplot
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|3|4|5|6"
#| output-location: fragment
lasso_tune |>
    collect_metrics() |>
    ggplot(aes(penalty, mean, color = .metric)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
    facet_wrap(~.metric, scales = "free", nrow = 2) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
```

:::

::: {.fragment}
> Look for the $\lambda$ that **maximizes ROC AUC** *before* the curve starts to crash. That's your sweet spot.
:::

---

## Pick the best $\lambda$ candidate

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|4"
#| output-location: fragment
best <- lasso_tune |>
    select_best(metric = "roc_auc")

best
```

::: {.fragment}
> ✨ One number — our winning $\lambda$ candidate. **Don't commit yet** — let's see how it actually performs first. 🤔
:::

# 5️⃣ Sanity-Check Before Committing

## How does our chosen $\lambda$ *actually* do? 🔍

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|3|4"
#| output-location: fragment
texting_wf |>
    finalize_workflow(best) |>
    fit_resamples(resamples = analysis_folds) |>
    collect_metrics()
```

::: {.fragment}
> An honest, CV-estimated performance for our **single** chosen $\lambda$.
:::

---

## 🔄 This is your decision point!

::: {.incremental}
- 😀 **Metrics look good** → lock it in, evaluate on test. ✅
- 😬 **Metrics look bad** → **STOP**. Go back and re-tune. 🛑
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## 🚨 Important
Once you commit with `finalize_workflow()` → `last_fit()`, **you've used your test set**. No going back.
:::
:::

---

## What does "go back and re-tune" mean? 🔧

::: {.incremental}
- Try a **wider** or **finer** $\lambda$ grid.
- Add a different **metric** (e.g. `pr_auc` for imbalanced data).
- Try `mixture = tune()` (Elastic Net) instead of pure Lasso.
- Revisit your **recipe** — feature engineering matters.
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 **Iterating here is the *job*.** Most "good models" took 5–10 rounds of this loop.
:::

# 6️⃣ Finalize + Fit

## Looks good? Lock it in 🔒

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
final_wf <- finalize_workflow(texting_wf, best)

final_wf
```

::: {.fragment}
> `finalize_workflow()` plugs the best $\lambda$ into the original workflow. **Now we're committed.** ✅
:::

---

## Fit on the training set

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|4"
#| output-location: fragment
texting_fit <-
    fit(final_wf, data = analysis_train)

texting_fit
```
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
![](img/woddy_fit.gif){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

# 7️⃣ Evaluate on the Test Set

## `last_fit()` — the magic shortcut ✨

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2-6"
#| output-location: fragment
texting_last_fit <-
    last_fit(
        final_wf,
        split = analysis_split,
        metrics = metric_set(accuracy, kap, roc_auc, sensitivity, specificity)
    )

texting_last_fit
```

---

## Why `last_fit()` is so cool 🪄

::: {.callout-tip}
## One function, four guarantees
- ✅ Fits on **all** training data
- ✅ Predicts on the **test** set
- ✅ Computes metrics — once, honestly
- ✅ Impossible to accidentally cheat
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 **Use this everywhere** — every model, every project. Period.
:::

---

## Test-set metrics

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
collect_metrics(texting_last_fit)
```

::: {.fragment}
> 👀 Compare these to your CV metrics. They should be **in the same ballpark** — that means your model generalizes.
:::

---

## Test-set predictions

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1-4|6"
#| output-location: fragment
the_prediction <-
    texting_last_fit |>
    collect_predictions() |>
    select(-.config, -.row)

the_prediction
```

---

## Confusion matrix

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
the_prediction |>
    conf_mat(TextingDriving, .pred_class) |>
    autoplot(type = "heatmap")
```

::: {.fragment}
> **Diagonals** = correct calls. **Off-diagonals** = mistakes. With imbalanced outcomes, look at the *off-diagonals* honestly.
:::

---

## ROC curve

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
the_prediction |>
    roc_curve(truth = TextingDriving, .pred_1, event_level = "second") |>
    autoplot()
```

::: {.fragment}
> A curve hugging the **top-left corner** = excellent. The diagonal = random guessing.
:::

# 🌟 The Lasso Payoff

## Variable importance — who survived? 🏆

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| code-line-numbers: "1|3|4|5|6|7|9-13"
#| output-location: slide
library(vip)

texting_last_fit |>
    extract_fit_engine() |>
    vi() |>
    group_by(Sign) |>
    slice_max(Importance, n = 5) |>
    ungroup() |>
    ggplot(aes(Importance, fct_reorder(Variable, Importance), fill = Sign)) +
    geom_col() +
    facet_wrap(vars(Sign), scales = "free_y") +
    labs(y = NULL) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
```

---

## How to read this plot 👀

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you're looking at
- **POS** bars push the prediction *toward* texting-and-driving.
- **NEG** bars push it *away* from texting-and-driving.
- Predictors not shown were **shrunk to zero** by Lasso — automatically irrelevant. ✨
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 This plot is your **headline figure** for the manuscript. 📝
:::

## Inspect the (sparse) coefficients

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
texting_fit |>
    extract_fit_parsnip() |>
    tidy() |>
    filter(estimate != 0) |>
    arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))
```

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 Many rows you started with are gone. Lasso did the **feature selection** for you.

## Step 2 — Swap the spec 🔄

::: {.incremental}
4. Change the spec to Lasso:
   ```r
   logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) |>
       set_engine("glmnet")
   ```
5. Add `tune_grid()` + `select_best()` + the **CV sanity-check** with `fit_resamples()`.
6. Then `finalize_workflow()` → `last_fit()`.
:::

# 🎁 Wrapping Up

## What you learned this session

::: {.incremental}
- ✅ **Why** we shrink coefficients — overfitting & high variance.
- ✅ **Ridge** (L2) keeps everything, **Lasso** (L1) drops things, **Elastic Net** does both.
- ✅ The **penalty** $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter — pick it with **cross-validation**.
- ✅ The full pipeline in `tidymodels`: split → recipe → spec → workflow → **tune** → finalize → fit → evaluate.
- ✅ How to read a **variable-importance plot**.
- ✅ Same shape as yesterday's pipeline. **One spec change**, brand-new model. ✨
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 You've now seen the full **tune → finalize** loop. Every algorithm tomorrow uses the **exact same shape**. 💪
:::
